title: AARO told the WSJ the shutdown was an EMP test

tellings.quote: so that they were able to tell Joel Sheckchman that this was some sort of EMP test.
Kirkpatrick’s team dug into the story and discovered a terrestrial explanation.
To test this vulnerability, the Air Force developed an exotic electromagnetic generator that simulated this pulse of disruptive energy without the need to detonate a nuclear weapon.
When activated, this device, placed on a portable platform 60 feet above the facility, would gather power until it glowed, sometimes with a blinding orange light.
The electromagnetic pulses snaked down cables connected to the bunker where launch commanders like Salas sat, disrupting the guidance systems, disabling the weapons and haunting the men to this day.

plain: In 2025 the Pentagon's UFO office is said to have told The Wall Street Journal that a famous shutdown of nuclear missiles, long blamed on a UFO, was really a secret Air Force test. Robert Salas, a former Air Force officer who says he was in the launch bunker in Montana when the missiles went down, tells Michels that the office was "able to tell Joel Sheckchman that this was some sort of EMP test". An EMP is an electromagnetic pulse, the burst of energy from a nuclear blast that can knock out electronics. The office is AARO, the Pentagon's current UFO office, then led by Sean Kirkpatrick. Joel Schectman's article in the Journal, published 6 June 2025, says "Kirkpatrick's team dug into the story and discovered a terrestrial explanation". It says the Air Force built "an exotic electromagnetic generator" to mimic the pulse, set "on a portable platform 60 feet above the facility", which "would gather power until it glowed, sometimes with a blinding orange light", and whose pulses "snaked down cables" to the bunker, "disabling the weapons". The article says it rests on "interviews with two dozen current and former U.S. officials, scientists and military contractors involved in the inquiry". The Defense Department statement it quotes is about fake classified program materials, not the shutdown. So saying that AARO as an office gave the Journal this account is Salas's reading of the reporters' unnamed sources, which the text neither confirms nor rules out.

discussion.by: The Pentagon Disinformation That Fueled America's UFO Mythology (The Wall Street Journal, 2025)
discussion.text: The article reports the EMP test as what "Kirkpatrick’s team dug into" and found, AARO under Sean Kirkpatrick, and says its account rests on "interviews with two dozen current and former U.S. officials, scientists and military contractors involved in the inquiry"; the Defense Department statement it quotes, from spokeswoman Sue Gough, is about fake classified program materials, not the missile shutdown. That AARO as an office told the Journal of the EMP test is the teller's reading of the reporters' sources, which the text neither names nor excludes.
